title: Mutable StringBuilder key in HashMap — lookup fails
shortTitle: What happens with a mutable StringBuilder key in HashMap?

s1_definition.profdef: Using a `StringBuilder` as a HashMap key is broken on two counts. First, StringBuilder does not override `equals` or `hashCode`, so it uses Object identity — two StringBuilders with the same text are different keys. Second, StringBuilder is mutable, so if you change its contents after inserting it, its `toString` changes but the entry stays in the bucket computed from the original state, and the lookup fails.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine labelling a drawer with a pencil-written tag that you later erase and rewrite. The filing clerk remembers which shelf the drawer went on based on the ORIGINAL tag; after you rewrite it, nobody can find the drawer any more. Use a permanent printed label (an immutable String) instead.
s1_definition.oneliner: Never use a mutable StringBuilder as a map key; use immutable String because it defines equals/hashCode and never changes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Using a `StringBuilder` as a HashMap key is broken on two counts. First, StringBuilder does not override `equals` or `hashCode`, so it uses Object identity — two StringBuilders with the same text are different keys. Second, StringBuilder is mutable, so if you change its contents after inserting it, its `toString` changes but the entry stays in the bucket computed from the original state, and the lookup fails.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine labelling a drawer with a pencil-written tag that you later erase and rewrite. The filing clerk remembers which shelf the drawer went on based on the ORIGINAL tag; after you rewrite it, nobody can find the drawer any more. Use a permanent printed label (an immutable String) instead.

**One line to remember:** Never use a mutable StringBuilder as a map key; use immutable String because it defines equals/hashCode and never changes.

sections.s3_banking: At the National Bank of India this came up directly when handling mutable StringBuilder keys in HashMap. Rajesh holds savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees and Priya holds current account CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees, and the team needed the collection behaviour to be exactly correct so balances and account lists were never wrong. The runnable demo below reproduces the situation and proves the behaviour with a small test.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A StringBuilder makes a terrible HashMap key because it relies on Object identity for equals and hashCode and because it is mutable. Changing the builder after insertion leaves the entry stranded in the bucket computed from its original contents, so lookups silently fail.

In the National Bank cache layer I enforced that every map key be immutable with value-based equality, using String account identifiers such as SAV2001 and CUR3001 and BigDecimal amounts. This avoided a whole class of bugs where a mutated key would make an account's cached data effectively disappear, which in a banking system could mean a balance lookup returning nothing at all.

In an interview I would stress that I always use BigDecimal for money, keep map keys immutable, and pick the collection whose ordering and complexity match the banking access pattern, because in a system that moves real money, choosing the wrong data structure is not a style issue, it is a correctness and reliability issue.

keyPoints: StringBuilder.hashCode() changes when content changes — lookup fails
After put, if you modify the key, get() returns null for the same object
HashMap cannot find the entry — it looks in the wrong bucket
Fix: never use mutable objects as HashMap keys — use String instead
